ingredients.intro: There is one botanical on this listing and there is no second one. Here is the species, what the label says about the material in the capsule, and the two places where it says nothing.

cards.alt: Phyllanthus niruri, small leaves in two ranks with round seed capsules hanging underneath the branchlets
cards.p: An annual herb of the wet tropics, rarely more than 60 cm tall. The small oblong leaves sit in two ranks along each branchlet, so a whole branch reads at a glance like one pinnate leaf. The tiny flowers and the round seed capsules hang underneath the branchlet rather than above it, which is the quickest way to place the genus in the field. It grows across South America, the Caribbean, West Africa and South Asia.

cards.alt: Clove buds, black peppercorns and a pale flecked powder in three small bowls on a wooden sill, a generated scene
cards.p: Chanca piedra reaches the trade as the whole aerial plant, the part above the ground, dried and milled. Our listing names the species and not the part, so this page does not name one either. The bowls in the picture are a generated scene and none of the powder in them is ours.

cards.alt: Loose capsules and a wooden scoop on dark slate
cards.p: The listing calls the contents an extract and gives no extraction ratio, which is the number that says how much dried plant went into a gram of powder. Without it, an extract is a word rather than a strength. We print the 800 mg because it is printed, and we do not print a ratio because there is not one to print.

cards.alt: Two plain capsules on a saucer beside a glass of water, a generated scene
cards.p: The listing describes a vegan friendly capsule and does not say what the shell is made from, so the sheet below does not name a material. The capsules in the picture are a generated scene rather than a photograph of ours.

Phyllanthus niruri L., family Phyllanthaceae. Older books file the genus under Euphorbiaceae. The listing prints the binomial and it is the accepted one.

Not printed. The listing places the plant in South America, which is where the species grows. It does not say where the material in this jar was grown or gathered, and we will not name a country we cannot evidence.
The listing names four plant compounds and gives a quantity for none of them. A name without a number is not a specification, so the compounds are not on this sheet.
Two capsules in the morning with at least 500 ml of water, and two in the evening with a meal and another 500 ml. That is four capsules in a day and it is the printed ceiling.
The listing prints no storage instruction. Keep the jar closed, cool and dry, out of the sun. It does not need a fridge.

doctrine.h3: We publish the specification. We do not publish claims about what it does.
doctrine.p: The species is named in Latin, the milligrams are printed, and the three figures we do not have, the count, the part of the plant and the extraction ratio, are named as missing rather than filled in. What chanca piedra does in a person is not something we are permitted to say. Neither is the name of the plant, which is why the name is left alone on this page.

reiss.label: Reiss's turn
reiss.h2: Why this page leaves the name alone
paras: Chanca piedra is what the plant is called in Peru and in Brazil, and the name has a plain meaning in Spanish. I am not going to print that meaning, because the meaning is a claim, and a claim in another language is still a claim. The name goes on the jar as a name. That is the whole of the work it does here.

What I can print is short. One plant, named in Latin. Eight hundred milligrams in a capsule. Two capsules in the morning, two in the evening, a big glass of water with each pair. Everything else on the sheet is a line about what the label does not tell me, and the one that annoys me most is the capsule count. Until that number is printed I cannot give you a cost a day, and I would rather leave the line blank than round one up and hope.

A herb this widely used should have more printed on it than this. The reason it does not is that it arrived in the trade as a tradition rather than as a specification. Traditions travel well and cost nothing to carry. Numbers have to be measured, and measuring costs money that a shop this size spends one label at a time.
reiss.pull: A claim in another language is still a claim.
